name: Fucoxanthin

lead: Fucoxanthin is an orange-brown carotenoid found in brown seaweeds such as wakame. Supplements, often seaweed or microalgae extracts, are sold for fat loss and metabolic health, with abdominal fat as the main target.

The pitch grows from rodent experiments, notably a 2005 study showing lower abdominal fat in animals fed lipids from Undaria pinnatifida, with higher expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in white fat. Human data are limited to a few small trials, and studies indicate low bioavailability.

paras: It is taken as capsules of seaweed or microalgae extract, typically alongside diet and exercise. The compound is sensitive to light, heat and oxygen, so product quality varies.
Reviews report it to be well tolerated in animals, and seaweed has long been eaten as food. Human safety data for concentrated supplements are limited.

angle.text: Supplement users take fucoxanthin, a brown-seaweed pigment, to burn fat and cut abdominal fat. The idea comes from rodent studies in which it raised fat-burning protein activity in white fat; human data are limited and absorption appears low.

lead: Fucoxanthin is a xanthophyll carotenoid (C42H58O6) that serves as a light-harvesting accessory pigment in brown macroalgae and diatoms, and gives them their olive-brown colour. It was first isolated in 1914 by Willstatter and Page from brown algae. [1][2]

Interest in fucoxanthin as an appearance-related supplement began with rodent studies reporting less abdominal white fat and increased UCP1 expression after feeding lipids from the edible seaweed Undaria pinnatifida. [3] Reviews describe additional antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and anticancer activity, mostly in cells and animals. [4][5]
Wikipedia notes that limited human studies indicate low bioavailability. [1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that large human trials are scarce. [2]

paras: Fucoxanthin contains an allenic bond, an epoxide, hydroxyl groups and a conjugated carbonyl group. It absorbs blue-green to yellow-green light with a peak at about 510 to 525 nm. [1] In diatoms it is the dominant carotenoid and can reach higher concentrations than in seaweed, which is the basis for industrial production in photobioreactors. [1][6]
It is fat-soluble and is reported to degrade with light, heat and oxygen. [2]

A review of fucoxanthin's metabolism and bioactivities describes its conversion to metabolites in the body and reports antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and anti-obesity actions in laboratory models. [4] Laboratory studies show radical-scavenging activity and suppression of NF-kB and MAPK inflammatory signalling in macrophage cells. [7][8]
The 2005 study found reduced abdominal white adipose tissue weight and UCP1 expression in white fat of rats and mice, which the authors proposed as a route to anti-obesity effects. [3]

Human research is limited. Registered trials include a Phase 2 study of fucoxanthin in metabolic syndrome, insulin sensitivity and insulin secretion (NCT03613740, 28 participants), a fucoxanthin-rich supplement for fatty liver (NCT03625284, 30 participants), and trials of a microalgae extract (Phaeosol) combined with exercise in overweight women (NCT04761406, 60 participants). [9][10][11] Results are not described in the sources available here. Wikipedia reports that limited human studies suggest low bioavailability. [1] Grokipedia states that only one obesity-focused trial was reported between 2017 and 2022. [2]

Grokipedia reports no mortality or genotoxicity in rodents at high doses and notes long dietary use of seaweed. [2] Wikipedia lists hazard statement H319 (serious eye irritation) for the pure compound. [1]

timeline.event: Willstatter and Page first isolate fucoxanthin from brown algae. [1]
Study reports reduced abdominal fat and UCP1 expression in white fat in rodents fed Undaria lipids. [3]
Review of metabolism, safety and bioactivities published in Marine Drugs. [4]
Phase 2 registered trial of fucoxanthin in metabolic syndrome starts. [9]
